Refugiul meu, furtuna mea

Arundhati Roy, Alexandra Coliban (Translator)

4.37
44,182 ratings6,433 reviews
Rate this book
Goodreads Choice Award
Nominee for Readers' Favorite Memoir (2025)
Primul volum de memorii al lui Arundhati Roy, Refugiul meu, furtuna mea, urmărește, cu forța narativă a romanelor sale și cu luciditate, evoluția uneia dintre cele mai puternice autoare ale literaturii contemporane. Acoperind perioada dintre 1962 și 2022, cartea reconstituie traseul interior al unei conștiințe în formare: copilăria fracturată, ruptura necesară, anii de rătăcire fertilă și, în cele din urmă, apariția romancierei și eseistei. Scrise sub impactul unei pierderi decisive, memoriile sunt mai puțin o elegie și mai mult un act de clarificare, o încercare de a înțelege cum se naște o voce, cum se cucerește libertatea și ce preț cere adevărul. Titlul original, Mother Mary Comes to Me, trimite la un vers celebru din piesa Let It Be a formației Beatles, dar și la Mary Roy, mama scriitoarei, pentru care a trăi după regula lui „nu-i nimic“ era de neconceput. Figura mamei rămâne un catalizator esențial al aces­tei deveniri: autoritară, vizionară, imposibil de ignorat, o forță redutabilă din care se alimentează scrisul lui Arundhati Roy. Alternând introspecția cu reflecții tăioase despre India, Refugiul meu, furtuna mea este o reconstrucție dureroasă și aproape sacră: o carte despre formarea eului artistic, despre dragostea care rănește, despre rădăcini și despre momentul fragil în care o viață se transformă în roman.

About the author

Arundhati Roy

122 books16.2k followers
Arundhati Roy is an Indian writer who is also an activist who focuses on issues related to social justice and economic inequality. She won the Booker Prize in 1997 for her novel, The God of Small Things, and has also written two screenplays and several collections of essays.

For her work as an activist she received the Cultural Freedom Prize awarded by the Lannan Foundation in 2002.

The Booker Prize held no meaning for me before I read Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things; I came to understand it as a marker of extraordinariness because that extraordinary novel had won it. To this day, I measure my liking for Booker-awarded works by whether or not they hold up to the experience of reading about Estha, Rahel, and Pappachi's Moth – very few ever do.

Roy is known today not just for the brilliance of her fiction – screenplays like In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones and Electric Moon which preceded The God of Small Things, and The Ministry of Utmost Happiness , which followed a decade after – but also her commitment to left-wing political activism and the powerful, prescient – almost clairvoyant – non-fiction borne from it. Now, in this first work of memoir, she takes us through the story of how she became the writer, activist, and person she is, shaped a little by circumstance and a lot by her complex relationship with her mercurial mother.

Though not as well-known as her daughter, Mary Roy was too a remarkable woman: a formidable feminist and an inspiring educator who transformed many lives in Kerala. However, she too was not without her flaws. Mother Mary Comes to Me reveals the fullness, trouble and tumult, of her legacy through the eyes of her 'valiant organ-child'. As it follows the separate but interminally linked journeys of the two women, Mary and Arundhati, it shapes up into an unflinching, honest portrait of the complexity and irreducability of human relationships – of love.

Roy's writing here is beautiful and passionate, threaded through with characteristic humour and political clarity, and an uncharacteristic sense of candour. Long-time fans will delight as much in learning more about the author's unconventional and hitherto closely-guarded private life as in the manifold insights this book provides into the process and passage through which all her works – including Walking with the Comrades, her commanding account of a year spent among Naxalite (Maoist) guerrillas deep within the forests of rural Chattisgarh – have come about. New readers will find themselves taken by her lucid brilliance and her lived philosophy of language, the world, the writing life and beyond.

A must read.

In a Nutshell: A memoir written by one of India’s most eloquent writers. I picked it up for her writing and was rewarded richly with her thoughts and words. Her deeds aren’t always my cup of tea, but I judge memoirs by their content and not by their authors’ life choices. This was an easy winner in that regard. Much recommended.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

I am not a big fan of memoirs. I find most of them fake and pretentious and even indulging in humble-bragging. Celebrity memoirs are even worse because they all sound the same (probably because most of them are ghostwritten by the same ghostwriters who went to the same kind of creative writing courses.) I also am not a big fan of the new trend in memoirs wherein dirty family linen is washed in public, sometimes after the death of the “antagonist”. Given all this, I shouldn’t even have picked this book up, forget about reading it. But there was one key differentiating factor to this book that swung my vote in its favour: its author.

Arundhati Roy’s ‘God of Small Things’ is one of my all-time favourite novels. I don’t think any other book brought an Indian state (Kerala in this case) to such authentic life as this book did. It is the only book I consider a deserving Booker winner. (An award I otherwise hate as it always prioritises purple prose over everything else.)

Given Roy’s literary background, I knew this memoir wouldn’t be a ghostwritten work. Given my experience with ‘God of Small Things’, I knew that her pen has the magical skill of creating a visceral picture with her words. And given her tendency of calling a spade a spade, of being brave enough to stand up against those in authority, and of being a strong advocate of human rights even when the humans involved might be controversial, I knew that the book would have plenty of brain fodder to chew upon.

The only part I was slightly hesitant about was the fact that the central focus of the memoir seemed to be her complicated relationship with her mother. I am somewhat conservative in this regard: I don’t like private battles being made public. This is why I won't read memoirs such as ‘Spare’ by Prince Harry or ‘I’m Glad My Mom Died’ by Jeanette McCurdy, no matter how much acclaim they get. But something told me I could trust Roy to do justice to the topic, and my gut instinct was right.

The title was also a determinant in stirring my interest. ‘Let It Be’, written and sung by Paul McCartney, is among my favourite songs, and the title is taken from its second line. Roy’s mother’s name is Mary, but the coincidental shared name is not the only reason the title makes sense. The author illustrates through various anecdotes how her mother came/comes to her literally and metaphorically.

The book begins and ends with her mother’s death at the age of 89, bringing the memoir a complete circle. In between, Roy elaborates not just on the complex connection she shared with her mother but also her relationships with her other family members, her school and college years, her early work years, her journey towards ‘God of Small Things’, and life beyond her international success. She uses the technique of foreshadowing quite effectively to keep our interest maintained. Most of her anecdotes are chronological, making this a wonderfully structured memoir. The writing is erudite; the prose, exquisite.

Roy is a fair bit older than me, so I was unaware of her life before ‘God of Small Things’. (I had read it in the years before the internet and social media boom, so there was no online search to look up the author’s credentials.) As such, all the content in this filter-free memoir was quite a revelation to me. I had absolutely no idea that she was already a known name in certain fields before the Booker win. Her childhood and family background isn't from an India I know in time or place, so that was also fascinating to read. She comes from a family of intellectuals (on her maternal side), but their behaviour was not in correspondence with their education. As she spent most of her formative years with them, her personality and life choices were influenced by their behaviour to a great extent.

Further, even her mother was a somewhat reputed figure in their hometown, known for a legal battle fighting for daughters’ rights to parental property as well as for founding a school. Mary Roy’s fierce personality is explored in a nuanced way by her daughter. Neither is there any fingerpointing nor any varnishing of facts. Roy keeps her tone mostly neutral, focussing not on complaining or whining about her lot in life but on the life lessons gained from being her mother’s daughter. The memoir seems like a masterclass in maturity when it comes to talking about toxic parenting.

Of course, Roy is still quintessentially Indian, so when she talks about how she still felt anxious when her mother was unwell or how she kept contact with her alcoholic father who was clearly using her, we don’t judge her for being weak or duplicitous, but know that she is just “fulfilling her responsibility” to her parents as most people until our generation have been taught to. I don’t know if those outside India will understand this double-edged sword of duty even towards undeserving elders, but we Indians certainly do.

Given the number of decades this book covers and the varied fields Roy has been an active part of, this book isn't just a memoir but a glimpse into actual India. Gender discrimination, classism, religious bigotry, political power-wielding, legal conundrums, geographical variations, cultural differences, corporate greed – Roy covers it all, and without any apprehension about the consequences. What is most admirable is that she doesn’t take sides. She critiques anyone who she thinks is at fault, no matter which political party or religion or family they belong to. And all this without any needless name-dropping. She names only those people who had a direct connection with her (such as her family and close friends), and that too, only when necessary. She also doesn’t shy away from admitting her own mistakes and sharing her regrets.

While I loved her insights on almost every aspect, the chapters connected to ‘God of Small Things’ and the impact it had on her life were closest to my heart. There was much realism to the writing and the characters of ‘God of Small Things’. It’s only on reading this memoir did I realise how much inspiration Roy took from her actual life to create that fascinating world and its denizens. No wonder they felt so powerfully carved! Though I have read GoST four times, my last read was more than two decades ago. Now I feel a strong urge to revisit its beautiful pages. Who knows… I just might dig out my old paperback soon!


🎧 The Audiobook Experience:
The audiobook, clocking at 11 hrs 29 minutes, is read by the author herself. While I am not usually a fan of authors narrating their own works, I had no apprehension when I saw Roy’s name in the narrator column. She is an articulate speaker and hence the perfect choice of narrator. Moreover, the book contains several phrases in Malayalam and Hindi, so listening to these rendered fluently adds to the experience. (Every non-English line comes with an immediate translation, so no worries about comprehension.)


Overall, this was one rare occasion when a memoir not only entered my TBR but also surpassed every single expectation I had from it. This book delivers on the parameters of engaging content, truthful admissions, intricate family drama, lyrical writing, structured organisation, historical and political milestones, and most of all, on the tricky thread connecting a mother and a daughter.

Much recommended to anyone looking for a truthful memoir that speaks at both a personal and a societal level.

4.5 stars, happy to round up.


Disclaimer: I rate memoirs just like I rate every other book: on writing quality. The actions and beliefs of the author have no role to play in my rating.

This was such a great book. In my undergraduate degree I studied writing, planned to become a writer, but never quite got there. My poetry was terribly overwrought and I wasn’t interested enough in form to be consistent. My short stories were a bit the same and the novel I started a bit disappointing. And then I decided that I didn’t understand the real world nearly enough to be going around inventing unreal ones. It was an idea that started as a seed and then grew and grew until I couldn’t really see around it. So, fiction troubled me. In my undergraduate degree my teacher was Gerald Murnane and he used to say – and probably still does – that fiction is the only time you can really know if someone is telling the truth. That if a character in a story that is telling you the story tells you that they believe what they are telling you is true – in a bit like Descartes telling you he is thinking and therefore he is – then you have no reason to doubt that what they are telling you is true. Yeah, yeah – dramatic irony and all that – but the point is that there is something that makes us trust fictional characters more than real life ones, where we are more likely to apply our irony detectors to the people around us than to those in fiction. But he also said somewhere recently (and by recently, maybe a book I read a decade ago) that he wished that he had never said which of his writings were essays and which were fictions. That the relationship between fiction and non-fiction was nowhere nearly as fine drawn as we pretend. I was saying this to Harsha today and realised that there is a contradiction between those two ideas – but perhaps more a Hegelian one, rather than a mathematical one. A productive contradiction rather than one that leaves only confusion.

My longtime ex, in all senses now, tried to get me to read The God of Small Things. She often did things like that. She’d started it and couldn’t go on, but wanted me to read it to tell her about it. She also tried to get me to read Descarte’s Bastards, but I resisted that one too. At least, I started Small Things, but it was too painful and I didn’t get more than a chapter or so in. I’ll probably have to read it all now. Roy would probably agree with Murnane about fact and fiction. She says as much in this at one point. This is, as it says on the cover, a book about her mother – although, really, it is an autobiography. I think if I were to write a book about my father it would be something similar to this. A man who loved me fiercely, but was fierce in his criticism of me too – not least because he had invested so much in me and was devastated by the idea I might end up going astray in some undefinable way. My mother told me that when I was too young to remember he would physically punish me for the smallest things. She was only able to stop him by saying that he would eventually break my spirit. But his disappointment was something I feared much more than any physical harm he might have done to me. And like Roy’s mother, I loved him back fiercely too. Even when I was far too old to justifiably want his praise, I went on wanting it.

Like Roy’s mother, my father is dead now too. But people who have had such a huge impact on your life are never really dead. He was an atheist, a rationalist, a Marxist – he would shake his head at my saying this, but his ghost is with me virtually every day. I don’t talk to him – we stopped talking years before he died. He stopped talking to everyone years before he died – other than within a very narrow range of topics, some political, but mostly about the weather. He was obsessed with sport and watched it endlessly – something I could never understand. But he lived it – shifting in his chair to avoid an oncoming tackle. Complaining when a player did something he felt was beneath them.

Roy has lived a fascinating life. You might think that upon becoming rich she would also become complacent – like the fabled people who become more conservative as they grow older – but that does not appear to be the case. As she says somewhere in this, she sees failure as a gift and success always reminds her that someone else, somewhere else, is being punished while she is being praised. I can’t help feeling I know exactly what she means.

My son-in-law sent me a photo of me holding my new granddaughter the other day – my first grandchild – she is utterly beautiful, just starting to learn to smile, so contented and pensive. I was struck by how old I look in the photograph, not at all as I think of myself – what they call in The Matrix my residual self-image, always much younger than I actually am. Perhaps we never grow up. Perhaps we are always awaiting the praise and censure of our parents, even after they are dead and gone and can no longer offer either.

This really is a remarkable book. Remarkable enough to make me need to read more of her writing. And, of course, having been brought up a Beatles nut, I’ve had Let It Be playing in my head for days while I’ve read this. Ah well, better than the shite that normally gets caught in my head.

“It has taken me years to come to terms with the fact that I was a middle child, one of three siblings, not two. My older sibling was a boy, and my younger sibling was a school. There was never any doubt about who our mother’s favourite child was. She loved, fought for and protected her youngest child with everything she had. That kind of focused, ferocious love, regardless of what it may choose as its object, is a blessed love. The challenge for those of us who are not chosen, and instead watch love pass us by, is to learn from it, marvel at it, and not grow bitter and incapable of love ourselves.”

Because I was too young to understand it when I lived in India, from seven to eleven years old, I was shielded from its heart of darkness. I only received the colors, the smells, the exuberance, the unabashed over-the-topness, the wild teeming streets, the loud festivities of Holi and Diwali, the pulsing rush of everything.

When I returned for a visit by myself at seventeen, the dark underbelly of that great, infinitely complex nation began to emerge, hidden in leering looks in market places, hidden in plain sight at each traffic light, where the poorest and the downtrodden came pleading with their eyes on the other side of your car windows. Abject inequality and sordid caste systems punching through the veil.

How the miracle that is Arundhati Roy bloomed from the fires of her childhood is something I will never understand and understand only too well. It is the same fire-fed genius that we see in Sinéad O’Connor, Billie Holiday, Bruce Springsteen or Karl Ove Knausgård. Renegade artists who never felt safe and met the world head-on with hungry hearts and a bone-deep aversion to injustice.

Arundhati is of the same breed. Armed with the most delicious and wicked sense of repartee and a cigarette perched at the corner of her lip, watch her make (no) sense of the formidable mother she calls her gangster and her storm. From the small villages of Kerala to the world stage of the Booker Prize, this is a literary promenade for the ages. Perhaps more than anything else, a tour de force in humanity.

I am completely floored by, enamored with and forever in awe of this gangster’s ardent daughter.

Arundhati Roy is savage. But so was her mother. When I was done reading the book, it unsettled me that an activist as fierce as Arundhati often shrank before her mother’s ridicule. The rebel in me sighed in relief when she finally snapped back and broke a chair in response to one of Mary Roy’s outrageous demands. But by then she had already slipped into a senile cognitive decline.

The God of Small Things was one book that had left me nostalgic for parts of Kerala I barely knew, and when in Mother Mary Comes To Me, Arundhati Roy describes how everything including electric poles is smothered with plants and creepers I was easing into loving the beauty that greenery gives Kerala. But was reminded with a jolt that toxicity too thrives in that lush. I could absolutely relate when she wrote of Delhi as her liberation from a life she shudders to think of.

At its heart, the memoir is about a daughter’s unconditional love, reverence and adoration for her brilliant but cruel mother. However, much of the book actually explores personal anecdotes, mother daughter dynamics, life of children in her mother's school, political injustices in Kashmir, Naxalism in Jharkhand, the whirlwind success of The God of Small Things, the back stories of her published work, the wave of political changes in India in the 90s...blending the trivial and the profound.

The result is a beautiful account that is deeply personal, politically insightful and a stylistically unforgettable smooth read that felt like cutting into a layered cheesecake. Yum!

Arundhati Roy’s writing, at its best, is vivid, lyrical, and powered by moral urgency. She seems to thrive when writing about the issues she cares most deeply about—caste, Kashmir, the Narmada Bachao movement—where her anger at structural injustice turns into ammunition. Lines like “A man’s life was prescribed as medication to soothe a maddened nation” remind us of her ability to compress political fury into poetry.

The book’s central subject is Roy’s relationship with her mother, Mary Roy, and the ambiguous grief she experiences after her death. This is an intensely personal project, and it feels slightly inappropriate to critique a book that is, at heart, an act of mourning. I will do it nevertheless as a way to process what I read.

After the book’s overwhelmingly positive reception, I approached it expecting to be moved and to gain insight into how Roy’s childhood, relationships, and losses shaped her as a writer, activist, and intellectual.

What I encountered instead was a disappointingly one-sided portrait. While the book offers a detailed and unsparing account of Mary Roy’s flaws and contradictions, it presents very little introspection about Arundhati Roy herself. Her internal journey—the self-questioning, uncertainty, or transformation one might expect from a memoir—is largely absent. The emotional lens is fixed outward rather than inward. This struck me as an odd choice.

However, what is most striking is how much of Roy’s life appears to unfold through coincidence and good fortune. Opportunities simply seem to materialize. She happens to meet a man who casts her in a hit film; she happens to marry him and finds in him an admirer, creative partner, and lover; she happens to live in a grand house while her debut novel happens to win the Booker Prize. He happens to be the perfect man, complete with two daughters whose mother conveniently dies, allowing Roy to step seamlessly into the role of caregiver. An essay she happens to write and print out just happens to be lying around when a publisher stumbles upon it and declares it extraordinary. John Cusack, who happens to be her friend, casually suggests they co-author a book on Snowden.

These moments accumulate into a pattern where monumental success comes easy. Even her failures, when acknowledged at all, feel minor, romanticized, or quickly brushed aside. There is little sense of prolonged struggle or doubt. Roy rarely seems stalled or humbled for long before another milestone appears.

To her credit, Roy does acknowledge her privilege: her cosmopolitan, elite Syrian Christian upbringing, her uncle’s education at Balliol College, Oxford, her unconventional but progressive schooling. Yet these acknowledgments feel curiously disconnected from the trajectory of her success. She never fully interrogates how this social and cultural capital may have smoothed her path or expanded her margin for risk.

Perhaps most unsettling is the unwavering moral certainty that permeates the narrative. Roy presents herself as consistently guided by justice, fairness, equality, and an unerring sense of ethical “goodness.” She does not appear to wrestle with moral ambiguity, compromised choices, or internal contradictions. This level of self-assured righteousness, especially in a memoir, feels discordant to me.

In the end, Mother Mary Comes to Me left me feeling skeptical of Arundhati's truth. Yes, the prose is beautiful, and there are moments of sharp observation and emotional insight. But mostly, Roy’s story feels disingenuous, overly curated, and improbably lucky.

While the book offers a penetrating examination of a mother, it presents a surprisingly opaque portrait of the daughter. I, for one, just don't buy it. The almost complete absence of self-scrutiny feels like a missed opportunity and does little to endear Arundhati to her readers, in my opinion.

যে-হাস্যকর অন্ধ যুগে আমরা এখন বাস করছি, যখন একটি গণতান্ত্রিক রাষ্ট্রের নির্বাচিত সরকার তার দেশের মানুষদের থেকে দাবি করে নিরঙ্কুশ বশ্যতা (যেন গণতন্ত্র নয় রাজতন্ত্র চলছে)। দেশের মিডিয়ার সঙ্গে সরকারের সম্পর্ক যেন ভৃত্যের সঙ্গে প্রভুর, তবু সেই দেশের প্রধানমন্ত্রী (যিনি আবার একজন বিশ্বগুরুও বটে) তার পোষ্য মিডিয়ার সামনে দাঁড়িয়ে প্রেস কনফারেন্স করতে ভয় পান— গত ১২ বছরে একটাও করেননি। যেখানে রাষ্ট্র ফিকির খোঁজে কীভাবে এবং কতোরকমভাবে দেশের মানুষের থেকে ট্যাক্স আদায় করা যায়, কিন্তু দেশের মানুষ যখন শাসকের কাজকর্ম কিংবা চিন্তাভাবনা নিয়ে প্রশ্ন তোলে কিংবা সমালোচনা করে, তাকে সরাসরি "দেশদ্রোহী" তকমা দেওয়া হয় এবং পরামর্শ দেওয়া হয় দেশ ত্যাগ করে পাকিস্তান কিংবা বাংলাদেশে চলে যেতে। দেশের সেনাবাহিনী এবং বিচারব্যবস্থার প্রতি কোনো সমালোচনামূলক মন্তব্য করা নিষেধ (ঠিক যেমন ঈশ্বরের সমালোচনা করা নিষেধ), এবং করলে তৎক্ষনাৎ শাস্তি দেওয়া হয় (অথচ সুস্থ মাথার যেকোনো মানুষ প্রতিনিয়ত বুঝতে পারে যে, এই দুটো প্রতিষ্ঠান যতটা পবিত্রতা দাবি করছে ততটা পবিত্র তারা নয়)। যখন রাষ্ট্র সর্বতোভাবে দেশের সাধারণ মানুষের বদলে কতিপয় ব্যবসায়ীর স্বার্থ রক্ষা করতে বেশি উদ্যমী। যখন দেশের রাষ্ট্রপ্রধান নিজের মেরুদণ্ড বিকিয়ে পৃথিবীর স্বঘোষিত দুর্বৃত্তদের সঙ্গে নির্লজ্জ আঁতাত (নাকি আত্মসমর্পণ?) করতে ব্যস্ত। এরকম একটি অন্ধ সময়ে অরুন্ধতী রায় ক্রমাগত কথা বলে চলেছেন রাষ্ট্রের অপকর্মের বিরুদ্ধে (বিদেশ থেকে লুকিয়ে নয়, দেশের মাটিতে দাঁড়িয়ে)। বরাবর যেমন হয়, এবারেও তাঁর লেখা পড়ে পাঠক হিসেবে মনের ভেতর যে-দুটি ইমোশন জাগরূক হয়েছে তা হলো: গভীর দুঃখ এবং অক্ষম ক্রোধ।

নিজের আত্মজীবনীতে তিনি নিজেকে কেন্দ্রবিন্দুতে রাখতে চাননি। রেখেছেন তাঁর মা-কে। তাঁর মা এমন একজন মানুষ যাঁর ব্যাপারে তিনি বলেছেন: She was my shelter and my storm. শেল্টার কারণ নিজের ব্যতিক্রমী সাহস এবং দৃপ্ত চিন্তাভাবনার জন্য নিজের মা-কে কৃতিত্ব দিয়েছেন তিনি। স্টর্ম কারণ... এটা জানতে হলে বইটা পড়তে হবে। অরুন্ধতী রায়ের যেকোনো ইন্টারভিউ দেখলে দেখা যায় তিনি অনেক শক্ত-শক্ত কথা বলছেন অনুচ্চ একটি কণ্ঠস্বর এবং স্মিত একটি মুখচ্ছবি বজায় রেখে। তাঁর আত্মজীবনী পড়ে জানতে পারি, এই স্থৈর্যের শিক্ষা তিনি পেয়েছেন নিজের জীবন থেকেই। কারণ ঝোড়ো হাওয়ায় জাহাজ চালানোর সময় স্থির থাকাই সবচেয়ে বুদ্ধিমানের কাজ। অরুন্ধতী রায়ের জীবন তো একটা অবিশ্বাস্য ঝড়ের মতোই!

A song of love is a sad song
A song of love is a song of woe
Don't ask me how I know

ঝড়ের মুখোমুখি হয়েও জীবনকে তিনি ঘৃণা করেননি। কর্তব্য থেকে পালিয়ে যাননি। বইয়ের এক জায়গায় তিনি লিখেছেন: The world was too ridiculous for me to remain too sad for too long. একজন পিডোফাইল নিজের যৌন অপরাধ থেকে মানুষের মনকে দূরে সরিয়ে রাখার জন্য প্রায় তৃতীয় বিশ্বযুদ্ধ বাধিয়ে দিয়েছে— এমন একটি রিডিকিউলাস পৃথিবীতে সত্যিই খুব বেশিক্ষণ মুখ গোমড়া করে বসে থাকা সম্ভব নয়। কাশ্মীরের মানুষদের অসহায় ভবিতব্যকে চাক্ষুষ করে তিনি লিখেছেন: I could see cold anger and resentment being bottled up by people like money is banked in a capitalist economy. I felt their rage would mature with interest. Somehow. Some day. ভয়াবহ হাস্যকর এই পৃথিবীর সমস্ত নগ্ন অনাচারের বিরুদ্ধে অভিশপ্ত মানবজাতির চূড়ান্ত ক্রোধ কবে ফেটে পড়বে?

বিষয়বস্তু ছাড়াও অরুন্ধতী রায়ের গদ্য সবসময়ই আমার বিশেষ পছন্দের। অরুন্ধতীর গদ্য সুললিত অথচ স্পষ্ট। অন্তর্ভেদী অথচ চমৎকার সরস। লেখাকে উজ্জীবিত করার জন্য তিনি বাকচাতুরি কিংবা শব্দচাতুরির আশ্রয় নেন না। গোটা বইতে এক লাইনেরও অতিকথন নেই। একবারের জন্যেও পাঠককে preach করার চেষ্টা করেননি। যে-কথাগুলো সাহস করে কেউ বলতে পারে না, কিন্তু বলা জরুরি, সেই কথাগুলো বলার জন্য অরুন্ধতী যেন স্বতঃপ্রণোদিত হয়ে এগিয়ে এসেছেন। আত্মজীবনীতে নিজের ব্যতিক্রমী জীবনকে উন্মুক্ত করেছেন এবং উন্মুক্ত করেছেন পাঠকের চিন্তাভাবনাকেও। ফেসবুক, টিকটক, ইনস্টা, রিলস, মিম, ভ্লগ, স্ট্যাটাস, ট্রল, ফোটো-ডাম্প (ফেল্ট কিউট, মাইট ডিলিট লেটার), ব্রেকিং নিউজ, হ্যালো ফ্রেন্স, কেমন আছো গাইজ, ইয়োলো, ফোমো, "এই পোস্টটা টাইমলাইনে থাকুক"-মার্কা ন্যাকামি-অধ্যুষিত আজকের এই আপাদমস্তক নিম্নমেধা অগভীর ভানসর্বস্ব আত্মমুগ্ধ কুরুচিকর আক্রমণাত্মক গণসমুদ্রে অরুন্ধতী রায় একটি একক লাইটহাউজের নাম। তথাকথিত "দেশভক্ত" ভেড়ার পাল নিয়মিত "anti-national urban-naxal bitch" উপাধিতে ভূষিত করে তাঁকে আগেও দমিয়ে রাখতে পারেনি, ভবিষ্যতেও পারার কোনো চান্স আছে বলে মনে হচ্ছে না গাইজ!

An angsty 11 reviews behind while aiming to enjoy the process has proved challenging lately. This reader is a work in progress

I placed a hold on this memoir as The God of Small Things has been quietly simmering in my mind for much too long, I thought this may be a good intro.

Roy has lived big in all the ways. This detailed and deeply introspective journey into an enormously rich life touched me immensely. The intense and vivid storytelling, the harsh and intimate details of a complicated existence felt like a special gift to the reader due to the immeasurable level of intimacy. Roy’s story from the earliest is tragic, loving, overwhelming and confronting, all rolled into one hectic legacy. I found myself in awe, an appreciative listener. Her succinct prose in being able to articulate the push pull nature and insane relationship with her mother continuing after her death is what I will think of for a long time. The mourning of a mother who did not act in societal ways.

Narrating herself in a lyrical voice in which I inhaled added so much more. I gasped, I paused, always reflecting on her strength of character in dealing with an intensely complex mother. I didn’t capture quotes as I usually like to, but I did get one:
*Who suckle on mobile phones from the moment they are born. It is a generational thing.*
A tiny thread pulled from an enormous story, a full and extreme life surrounded by every contrast the mind can conjure. Wealth, poverty, love, abuse, corruption, education, articulation, destitution.

There is so much I do not understand in the world she inhibits, but in teaching me a lot, Arundhati Roy has grabbed my heart delivering this moving memoir from the depths of her soul. An amazing talent, gifted, resilient and funny woman. The funny that is borne out of necessity and a life well lived. My highest recommendation ~ and if you have read it do let me know x

I find myself in a somewhat unique position. I just finished Arundhati Roy’s breathtaking (that is, reading it took my breath away!) memoir, and yet I have not read anything she has previously written and published. My usual linearity-seeking compulsion is to read some, or all, books by an author, and then read a memoir or a solid, scholarly biography. I like to know what was going on in the author’s life when he or she wrote a particular book. Despite having turned my usual model upside-down by reading Ms. Roy’s memoir before any other of her works, my inclination to read everything she has written is still irresistibly strong.

Roy’s prose in the memoir is terse and unsentimental, written almost with brutal journalistic brevity. For readers, this means a fast pace, but without any danger of a stumble as it becomes a compulsive page-turner. The mother-daughter interactions don’t seem to happen often, but that could be the pace at which events move.

If nothing else, Mary Roy, Arundhati’s mother, was a force of nature, and even that is probably understating the case. She did everything with vim and vigor, and with an expectation that was more entitlement than optimism, that she would undoubtedly succeed in every undertaking—which she more-or-less did. Arundhati’s parents divorced when she was two, and Mrs. Roy promptly started a school on a shoestring budget. The only pains the school suffered seem to have been from rapid growth in physical size and scope of curriculum.

The relationship between mother and daughter was brittle at best; tough love would be a euphemistic characterization. The mother rarely had a kind word or gesture of affection for the daughter, and yet, their bond only seemed to strengthen with every prickly interaction—at least as Arundhati tells it. I have not a single doubt that she is a sincere and truthful memoirist.

Arundhati was clearly a smarter-than-average child: she succeeded academically as a child and graduated from a School of Planning and Architecture in New Delhi. She married husband number one in 1978 at age 17, but divorced him in 1982. She married husband number two in 1984 and, still in her twenties, achieved recognition in writing screenplays.

The activist gene that was clearly present in the mother inevitably appears in the daughter on steroids, and much of her later writing fell into that context. However, she knew, or sensed that she should be writing something else. Her first novel, The God of Small Things, was four-to-five years in the making, but Arundhati knew she was meant to write it, and everything that came before was apprenticeship for this book. It was hugely successful, winning the Man Booker Prize in its publication year. Thereafter, the majority of her writing consisted of essays, with a second novel, The Ministry of Utmost Happiness, appearing 20 years after the first.

I suspect Mother Mary Comes to Me will be as successful as anything else Roy has written, if not more so. It is truly a terrific story of family and everything that goes along with that: happiness, joy, sadness, pain, success, disappointment; and if love seems absent or occasionally sacrificed, it is resoundingly redeemed at the end. I have consumed numerous memoirs over decades of reading—this one ranks as one of the best!

★ ★ ★ ★

"This book didn't change my politics. It exposed the fact that I don't have one."

There are books you finish with answers. Then there are books that quietly dismantle the illusion that you ever had them.

Reading Mother Mary Comes to Me was a strange experience. I came for Arundhati Roy the novelist—the woman whose sentences have always felt alive, whose observations are so precise that even silence seems to have a voice. I stayed for the deeply personal reflections on her mother, her childhood and the making of the woman behind the public figure.

Then the politics arrived.

As an Indian reader, I don't think I experienced this book the way many international readers will. Outside India, Roy is often read as a fearless dissenter, and understandably so. But within India, she is one of the most polarising public intellectuals of our time. She has been called everything from a revolutionary to an anti-national, and those labels carry histories that can't be understood without understanding India itself.

That's where this book unsettled me.

Not because I agreed with everything she wrote. Not because I disagreed either. But because I realised I wasn't politically educated enough to do either with confidence.

It's easy to rate this book five stars if you approach it already convinced by Roy's worldview. It's equally easy to dismiss it if you've already rejected her. The harder position—and the one I unexpectedly found myself in—is admiration without certainty.

I admire her courage. I admire her prose. I admire the way she preserves memory and gives dignity to lives history often ignores. But admiration isn't the same as agreement, and this book forced me to confront that distinction.

India's politics isn't a neat morality play. It isn't simply good versus evil, left versus right, nationalism versus dissent. It is layered, contradictory and emotionally exhausting. Roy presents one moral vision of that complexity. Whether you embrace it or reject it, I think you owe it to yourself to understand the arguments before choosing a side.

Ironically, this book has convinced me not to adopt Roy's politics, but to finally begin studying politics seriously. If I ever arrive at a political worldview, I want it to be one I've earned—not one I've borrowed from my favourite writer.

For that reason alone, this is a four-star read.

Not because it changed my mind.

Because it made me realise I hadn't fully made it up yet.

“I left my mother not because I didn’t love her, but to be able to continue to love her. Staying would have made that impossible. Once I left, I didn’t see or speak to her for years. She never looked for me. She never asked me why I left. There was no need for that. We both knew. We settled on a lie. A good one. I crafted it. ‘She loved me enough to let me go.’ That’s what I said at the front of my first novel The God of Small Things which I dedicated to her. She quoted it often, as though it were God’s truth. My brother jokes that it’s the only piece of real fiction in the book.”

“As a child I loved her irrationally, helplessly, fearfully, completely, as children do. As an adult I tried to love her coolly, rationally, and from a safe distance. I often failed. Sometimes miserably. I wrote versions of her in my books, but I never wrote ‘her’. She liked those versions though and embraced the character of Ammu in The God of Small Things whom she would refer to as ‘I’ and ‘me’. She wanted to be Ammu because she knew very well that she wasn’t.”

************
Arundhati Roy first became well known for her 1998 Booker Prize winning novel ‘The God of Small Things’. It was a brilliantly written description of her childhood in Aymanam, a southern town in Kerala, India. This memoir, published nearly a quarter century later, reveals an interesting contrast between factual and fictional accounts by the same author. If there is any doubt Roy’s novel is biographical it is dispelled. Each character has real life twin, except for Rahel’s fictional twin Estha, who actually is her older brother LKC. People, places and events surrounding sex scandals of her mother and brother are from her imagination.

Both novel and memoir are clear and unsentimental views of her life. The writing has style, depth and humor. Her mother was a well known activist who fought for the inheritance rights of Indian women. Her socialist uncle owned a pickle factory and harassed the female workers. Mrs Mathews, a British missionary, and Mary opened a boarding school which Roy and her brother attended. Her father was an alcoholic who Mary divorced when Roy was two. Although fallen on hard times the family was better off than many. Mary’s school challenged traditional gender roles and is a popular and progressive institution in Kerala.

Her virtues aside, ‘Mother Mary Comes to Me’ is not the Life of a Saint. There are numerous stories of her abrasive and uncompromising nature. Being male, LKC bore the brunt of her anger against her abusive former husband and dead father who often beat her mother with a brass vase. Merely average test scores would occasion a thrashing with a cane. Roy’s own nearly perfect scores filled her with guilt and were the grounds for epic battles between the siblings. She comments on India being ‘a land of son worshippers’ where male offspring are given more of everything. In this context it was sacrilege to take revenge on LKC.

Roy was not immune from the wrath of Mary however. She was ‘still a villager’, while her mother had grown up in Delhi, studied in Madras and married in Calcutta. In 1969, when Roy was nine she had her first memory of Naxolites, a Maoist revolutionary group from Bengal who beheaded their landlords. Her family were Christians who traced their faith back to the time of St. Thomas the Apostle. Christ’s views of the poor aligned with Communists, but none who converted from Hinduism to escape the caste system were allowed to join them. A main character Velutha in her novel was low caste and Naxolite, groups she advocated for.

In 1976 Roy finished boarding school and attended the Delhi School of Architecture, partly to get away from Mary and partly to explore sex, drugs and rock and roll, which wasn’t part of the curriculum at home. The memoir continues after events told in ‘The God of Small Things’, which is the story of her childhood. Even if the author isn’t the main interest it is informative of life in India during the period, set in Indira Gandhi’s emergency, sterilization of Muslim men, massacre of Sikhs in Amritsar and the Babri mosque demolition. Roy would eventually cut off communication with Mary, who had become too domineering to contend with.

Roy recounts her indigent marriage to a fellow architecture student, marriage and separation with the husband of her boss, who came with house, dogs and daughters. She starred in a Hindi movie without spoken lines, worked on historical restoration projects in Rome, became a screenwriter. At the time it was difficult for a single women to avoid groping and rape in India. Her life changed greatly with the publication of her first novel, which became a critical and commercial success. It wasn’t until seven years later in 1984 that she reconnected with Mary. Throughout all of her numerous challenges she was fearless as Mary had been.

Reading two accounts of the same events, the memoir is clearer but lacks some of the drama of the novel. It works as a companion text revealing the source of her inspiration and invention. Alone it is an autobiography which offers greater insight into Roy’s thoughts, freed from the demands of story telling. She is forthcoming and candid in her revelations. I feel I know her a little better now but have been infatuated for years. After ‘The God of Small Things’ she published one other novel. The rest of her work has been in nonfiction and political activism. She was charged with sedition in 2010 for her speech on Kashmiri independence.

I loved this audio book. It is the best of so many I have heard. I started listening to audio books in 1982 when I moved to NYC and walked over 2 miles to work each day with a walkman and cassette tapes for my companion. So I believe myself rather an expert in the field of audiobooks. This is one of the best and most beautiful in the many thousands I have listened too. It is read by the author herself with a soft, enchanting and most articulate voice. It was a pleasure to listen to.

As I age, now 76, I still listen but most often with the print in my hand to make sure I absorb the words and can find phrases I love (it is such a pain to go back and forth to try to bookmark in audio).

This was such a great memoir of Arundhati Roy and her relationship with her mother and India which helped to shape who she is. This relationship was fraught with not much warmth or apparent love, not always the easiest to write or read about. Yet there is so much beauty and great writing in this book. This story recounts Roy's early life, where she was educated at her mother's school. Her years in Delhi when she was largely estranged from her family. The relationships with her two husbands, the writing of her two novels, the first: The God of Small Things that won the Booker prize and her years of activism. There is a lot of history, her own and India's wrapped up in the 327 pages. My only criticism is I wish the print had more photos. One grainy photo appears on the end pages.

I also wish I had more of a knowledge of India. It would have enhanced my understanding of who she is and the protests and concerns she spends her days fighting for. Have to admit that a some of the activist chapters were over my head but I did get more background of the country than I had previously.

It is a wonderful memoir/auto-biography and I hope it finds a wide audience.

Two of my favorite quotes:

"He listened with his whole body. As though my words were rain, and he was the earth. He absorbed everything, gathered every drop...

"The balance in our relationship was upended. My newfound fame crashed into our little love tent and Jerked us around like puppets."


Note: I listened to the unabridged audio cassettes of the God of Small Things in about 1998 by Harper Collins. It is one of my all time favorite books which is what lead me to want to read this.

In 2016 I traveled for 3 weeks in India, my only visit to this most interesting of lands. I knew little of its history and had read God of Small Things, Midnight's Children, The White Tiger and A Fine Balance my only pre-trip fiction reading. Also read Beyond the Beautiful Forevers a non-fiction. Listening to this reminds me I need to read more fiction and non-fiction about this country which has so many people and history of its own. One thing that sticks with me about that visit was how important education is. Even for the poorest people living in metal shacks, I saw them in the early morning hours and late in the day holding hands with their young children who are in school uniform as they walked them down the side of a dusty road to school or coming home in dusk of the day. Roy's mother and her school was another example of this.

by the author herself.

Roy’s mother was a force to be reckoned with in more

the boys she taught to be kind and caring towards
women, but was abusive, harsh and cruel to her own children.

was sent away to bording school. Roy endured verbal
mental, and physical abuse. She often referred to her
mother as, “Mrs. Roy” instead of mother, mummy,
or mum which was very interesting and somewhat disconnected to me.

Arundhati did not compromise on anything
(something her mother taught her?) especially
with her writing, until she got full credit or equal billing.

I truly loved this audiobook and would love to visit Kerala, India where Roy is from.

অরুন্ধতী তার প্রথম বইয়ের জন্যেই বুকার পাইছিলেন। আর এই বইয়ের লঞ্চ যখন তার গ্রামে হইল, তার মায়ের প্রতিষ্ঠা করা স্কুলে, সেদিন সেখানে তার মামাকে আসতে দেখা গেল। অরুন্ধতীর মামার সাথে অরুন্ধতীর মামার ছিল বিবাদ। মেরি রায় (অরুন্ধতীর মা) যখন বালবাচ্চা নিয়ে কোট্টায়ামে এসে উঠলেন তখন তার মা (অরুন্ধতীর নানী) তাদেরকে থাকতে দিতে চায় নাই। এরপর মেরি রায় মামলা করে নিজের 'অধিকার' আদায় করে নিছিলেন। অরুন্ধতীর মামা আইজ্যাকের আচারের ব্যবসার লেজেগোবরে হইছিল বোনের জন্য। সে যা-ই হোক, বুক লঞ্চের সময় মামাকে আসতে দেখে অরুন্ধতীর মনে হইছিল আসর পণ্ড করতে আসতেছে মামা। কিন্তু আইজ্যাক কংস কিংবা শকুনি ছিল না। সে গিয়ে অরুন্ধতীর এজেন্টের সামনে দাঁড়াইয়া বলছিল, 'হ্যালো, আমি চাকো।' চাকো আসলে দ্য গড অফ স্মল থিংস-এর একটা চরিত্র। অরুন্ধতীর মামা অরুন্ধতীর বই পড়ছিলেন।

---
প্রথম বইটাই অরুন্ধতীর আত্মজীবনী থেকে উৎসারিত উপন্যাস। মাদার মেরি একদিকে অরুন্ধতীর আত্মজীবনী, অন্যদিকে তার মায়ের জীবনী। নিজের জন্ম থেকে এই পর্যন্ত সময়ের যাত্রা লেখিকা এইখানে রাখছেন কিন্তু তার প্রতিটা স্টেপ, ভয়, আনন্দ, অর্জন আর হারানোর সাথে রিলেট করছেন মা মেরি রায়কে। এই কারণে বইটা বিশেষ।

বইটা প্রকাশের পর বিভিন্ন সাক্ষাৎকারে বইয়ের অংশ, মায়ের অ্যাবিউজিভ আচরণ নিয়ে অরুন্ধতীর কথা বলা ইত্যাদি থেকে এমন একটা ভাইব আসছিল যে এইটা অরুন্ধতীর বই না, নেটফ্লিক্সের সিরিজ। তবে বাস্তবতা হইল এইটা অরুন্ধতীরই বই এবং এইটা পড়তে গিয়ে মেঘ, বৃষ্টি, রোদ, ধুলা, গাঁজার গন্ধের পাশাপাশি বিপ্লবের ধোঁয়া, প্রতিবাদের গর্জনও পাবেন। তবে আমার আপত্তির জায়গা একটাই।

অরুন্ধতী তার লেখক হয়ে ওঠার বিষয়টা খুব আলগোছে লিখছেন। অনেকটা এমন যে-গল্পটা আমার কাছে আইলো আর আমি লেইখা ফেললাম। অনেক সময় নিয়া কষ্ট কইরাই লিখছি কিন্তু সেইটা আসছে ভিতর থেকে। আসতে পারে, সমস্যা নাই। কিন্তু নর্মদা ড্যাম, ভারতের পলিটিক্স, কাশ্মীর নিয়া লেখা তো স্বপ্নাদেশের মাধ্যমে আসে না। প্রসুর পড়াশোনা করতে হয়, লাইনঘাট জানতে হয়। সেইসব অরুন্ধতী অবশ্যই করছেন। এইসব নিয়ে একখানা অন্তত চ্যাপ্টার থাকা উচিত ছিল, এই আরকি।

Obra híbrida, autobiográfica y ensayística, que narra la experiencia vital de Arundhati Roy, desde una perspectiva original, personal, y muy interesante. Creo que la valoro más por admiración intelectual y humana que por haberla disfrutado de una forma amena.

Su punto fuerte es la honestidad emocional y moral de la autora. 
Escribe desde una implicación absoluta con lo que cuenta: la enfermedad y muerte de la madre, la historia familiar, las tensiones afectivas, el peso político y cultural de la India, incluso la exposición de su propia figura pública. 
Eso evidencia la autenticidad de su voz.

La vida privada se entrelaza continuamente con su momento histórico, y muestra estructuras sociales, políticas y culturales muy valiosas que permiten una lectura del país, de la familia y del poder.

Pero...., algunos pasajes me han parecido muy explicativos, densos, poco narrativos, y a menudo ralentizan demasiado la lectura. Ha habido momentos en que me he aburrido.
Eso no quita para reconocer que incluso en esos momentos tiene detalles interesantísimos, algunos por ejemplo sobre la publicación de sus obras gustarán mucho especialmente a quien siga a la autora.

Desde luego no me ha parecido artificioso, que es mi temor en tantas obras de este tipo. La conciencia de sí misma como autora forma parte del del fluir narrativo y autobiográfico. Narra su vida, su duelo, su posición pública y su historia familiar desde una lucidez muy deliberada.

രേഖാ രാജിൻ്റെ അ അമ്മ എന്ന പുസ്തകം വായിക്കുമ്പോൾ അതിൽ രേഖ തൻ്റെ അമ്മയെ നിരന്തരം മനസ്സിലാക്കാൻ ശ്രമിക്കുന്ന ഒരു ജോലിയെക്കുറിച്ച് പറയുന്നുണ്ട്. വളരെ വലിയ രീതിയിലുള്ള അധ്വാനം ആവശ്യപ്പെടുന്ന ഒരു കാര്യമായാണതിനെ എഴുത്തുകാരി പറയുന്നത് - മാനസികമായും, ശാരീരികമായും, രാഷ്ട്രീയപരമായും. Mother Mary Comes to Me വായിക്കുമ്പോൾ നിരന്തരം രേഖയെയാണ് ഓർമ്മ വന്നത്. അനുഭവങ്ങളിലും അതു നടക്കുന്ന ക്യാൻവാസിലും അരുന്ധതി റോയ്ക്ക് വ്യാപ്തിയും വലിപ്പവും ഉണ്ടെങ്കിലും (ക്ലാസ്/കാസ്റ്റ് പ്രിവിലേജ് സാധ്യമാക്കുന്ന 'വലിപ്പം') രണ്ടുപേരും പറയുന്നത് ഏറെക്കുറേ ഒരേ കഥയാണ് (അല്ലെങ്കിൽ ജീവിതമാണ്). ബൈനറികളിൽ ഒതുങ്ങി നിൽക്കാത്ത, ശക്തമായ അകം/പുറം ജീവിതങ്ങളുള്ള, അമ്മയെന്ന ആർക്കിടെപ്പിൻ്റെ ഉള്ളിൽ ഒരിക്കൽ പോലും തങ്ങളെ കാണാനോ ഉൾക്കൊള്ളാനോ സാധിക്കാത്ത രണ്ട് സ്ത്രീകളെക്കുറിച്ച് അവരുടെ എഴുത്തുകാരികളായ പെണ്മക്കൾ (ഏറ്റവും കലുഷിതമായ അമ്മ - മകൾ ബന്ധത്തെക്കുറിച്ച്) എഴുതുന്നു. റോയ് പറയുന്നത് പോലെ അമ്മമാർ അവരുടെ കൂരയും കൊടുങ്കാറ്റുമാകുന്നു.

അമ്മയിലൂടെയാണ് റോയ് ജീവിതത്തെത്തന്നെ ഓർത്തെടുക്കുന്നത്. റോയ് എന്ന വ്യക്തിക്ക് സ്വന്തമായി ഒരു നിലനിൽപ്പുണ്ടോ എന്ന് പോലും നമുക്ക് സംശയമാണ്. അമ്മയ്ക്ക് ചുറ്റും രൂപപ്പെടുത്തിയ നിർമ്മിച്ചെടുത്ത ഒരു ശരീരവുമായാണ് അവർ ജീവിച്ചത്/ജീവിക്കുന്നത് എന്ന് പറയുന്നു. അമ്മയെ ഉൾക്കൊള്ളാനും ഉൾപ്പെടുത്താനുമായി അവർക്ക് കാലക്രമേണ രൂപാന്തരപ്പെടേണ്ടി വരുന്നു. അസാധാരണമായ രണ്ട് സ്ത്രീകളുടെ കഥയാണ്. ചില നേരങ്ങളിൽ എങ്കിലും അമാനുഷികം എന്ന് പോലും നമുക്ക് തോന്നിപ്പോകുന്ന അനുഭവങ്ങൾ ഉൾക്കൊള്ളുന്ന ഒരു പുസ്തകം. എങ്ങനെയൊക്കെയാണ് മനുഷ്യർ അവരുടെ ഏറ്റവും ക്രൂരമായ ഭൂതകാലങ്ങളേയും അതിലെ ഭൂതങ്ങളേയും നേരിടുന്നതെന്നും, ചിലതിനെ എങ്കിലും തുറന്നുവിടുന്നതെന്നും, മറ്റു ചിലതിനെ വേദനയുടെ കാവിൽ കൊണ്ടു പോയി തളക്കുന്നതെന്നും കാണാം. റോയ് വേദനയിൽ കിടന്ന് കരയുന്നില്ല. കരയാനോ നമ്മളെ കരയിക്കാനോ അവർക്ക് ഉദ്ദേശ്യവുമില്ല. ഒരു വേദനയെ അത് അർഹിക്കുന്നതിലും അപ്പുറത്തേക്ക് കടിച്ച് പിടിക്കാൻ അവർ ശ്രമിക്കുന്നുമില്ല. ഏതൊരു വ്യസനത്തെക്കുറിച്ച് പറയുമ്പോഴും റോയ് അവരുടെ പ്രിവിലേജുകളെക്കുറിച്ച് സ്വയം ഓർമ്മിപ്പിക്കുന്നു. വായനക്കാരെ നിരന്തരം ഓർമ്മിപ്പിക്കുന്നു. ആ ഓർമ്മിപ്പിക്കാൻ അവർ ഉപയോഗിക്കുന്ന ഭാഷ പോലും ഒരു പ്രിവിലേജിൻ്റെ ഭാഗമായി അവർക്ക് കിട്ടിയതാണ് എന്ന് വീണ്ടും ഓർമ്മിപ്പിക്കുന്നു.

റോയുടെ ഏറ്റവും വലിയ 'സ്വത്ത്' അവരുടെ ഭാഷ തന്നെയാണ്. ഒരിടത്തും അണകെട്ടിനിർത്താനാകാത്ത അത്രയും ഒഴുക്കുള്ള ഭാഷയാണ് ഈ ഓർമ്മക്കുറിപ്പുകളിലും. അവരുടെ നോൺഫിക്ഷൻ വായിച്ച ആളുകൾക്ക് രണ്ടാം പാതി ഒരു ടൈംലൈൻ ഡോക്യുമെൻ്റേഷൻ മാത്രമായി തോന്നാം. മറ്റു പുസ്തകങ്ങളിലും നീണ്ട ആർട്ടിക്കുകളിലും പറഞ്ഞിരിക്കുന്നത് ചെറിയ ചാപ്റ്ററുകളിലേക്ക് ഒതുക്കിയിരിക്കുന്നു എന്ന് പറയാം. പക്ഷെ അമ്മയെക്കുറിച്ച് പറയുന്ന ഭാഗങ്ങളെല്ലാം അതിതീവ്രമാണ്. അതു കൊടുങ്കാറ്റായും പേമാരിയായും വെള്ളപ്പൊക്കമായുമെല്ലാം വരുന്നു. പക്ഷെ ഒടുവിൽ, മുങ്ങിയ സ്ഥലങ്ങളിൽ വളക്കൂറുള്ള മണ്ണ് വന്നടിയുകളും അതിൽ മുളപൊട്ടുകയും ചെയ്യുന്നിടത്ത് റോയ് നിർത്തുന്നു. അവിടം അവർക്ക് തണലേകുന്ന ഒരു കാട് തന്നെ മുളയ്ക്കട്ടെ എന്ന് ആഗ്രഹിക്കുന്നു.
